paper_metadata.title: Smart Vault Security in Banks: A Quantum AI-Enabled Intrusion Detection System

summary: The paper presents a gate-based hybrid QSVM intrusion-detection system for bank smart-vault security using quantum feature encoding and quantum kernel methods. It reports 96.5% accuracy, 95.2% precision, 97.0% recall, 97.5% F1-score, and 0.98 ROC-AUC, outperforming a classical SVM baseline (about 90.5% accuracy, 89.2% precision, 91.0% recall), but only in simulation on a workstation with no named quantum hardware.

experiments.description: Hybrid quantum-classical intrusion detection for smart vault security using quantum feature encoding, quantum kernel computation, and QSVM classification on a real-world bank vault security dataset, with an additional synthetic dataset simulation reported for robustness and real-time performance.

algorithm.variant: Quantum kernel-based SVM (QSVM) with quantum feature encoding

hyperparameters.kernel: quantum kernel based on squared inner product of quantum states

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Classical features are mapped into quantum states using a parameterized unitary operator U(x); the implementation example uses a single-qubit rotation gate for a classical feature value, and the paper also mentions amplitude encoding in the methodology section.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Binary classification of normal vs intrusion events using a QSVM decision function sign(sum_i alpha_i y_i K(x_i, x_new) + b).

problem_instance.description: Bank smart vault intrusion detection using access logs, biometric data, sensor readings, and network traffic indicators.
problem_instance.dataset_name: Bank smart vault security dataset; synthetic dataset for supplementary tests

dataset_specification.description: Features include time interval between access attempts, authentication score, sensor anomaly score, and network traffic indicators; labels are normal or intrusion.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Missing values imputed using mean imputation; features normalized to [0,1]; data cleaned and normalized before encoding.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Performance measured on a test set using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and ROC-AUC; additional synthetic-data simulations reported; no explicit cross-validation protocol stated except C optimization via cross-validation.

implementation_details.classical_solver: scikit-learn SVM with custom quantum kernel
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Mean imputation and min-max normalization to [0,1].
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Thresholding QSVM decision function to label intrusion vs normal; alert generation and response triggering.

speedup_claims.caveats: The paper claims near-real-time detection and improved performance, but does not provide a formal computational speedup factor or asymptotic advantage.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Quantum feature encoding and kernel evaluation on a simulator/workstation; no QPU, no qubit count, and no asymptotic complexity or crossover analysis reported.
limiting_factors: Classical SVM baseline remains competitive and is explicitly used for comparison
No qubit count or circuit depth reported

notes: Hardware inferred as simulator_other because the paper states simulations were executed on a workstation and uses Qiskit/PennyLane statevector simulation, with no real QPU named.
Number of qubits is not explicitly reported; the paper describes single-qubit feature encoding examples and quantum state encoding generally, but does not specify total register size.
No asymptotic speedup order is characterized in the paper; only empirical performance improvements are claimed.
The paper reports improved empirical metrics for the proposed QSVM-based IDS, but does not establish a practical quantum advantage.
Reported results include 96.5% accuracy, 95.2% precision, 97.0% recall, 97.5% F1-score, and 0.98 ROC-AUC, with a classical SVM baseline around 90.5% accuracy, 89.2% precision, and 91.0% recall.
